yajña.text:
The word for the rite itself, and the most frequent of the terms that describe it — 469 verses. It is not confined to any one part of the collection: maṇḍala 10 carries the most (97) and maṇḍala 1 next (82), but every book has it, because every book is about it.

Its first appearance is the first line of the Ṛgveda. RV [[1.1]].1 calls Agni *purohitaṃ yajñasya devam* — the god placed in front of the yajña — so the reader meets the word before meeting anything else. What follows in that sūkta is the mechanism: what is given into Agni rises, and reaches those it was sent to.

The brāhmaṇa portion of the Veda is given over to how a yajña is performed — which officiants, in what order, with what formulae — and the saṃhitā supplies the mantras it uses. The two are portions of one Veda, and a term met in the mantra is set out in procedure in the manual. Compare {{adhvara}}, the other principal word for the rite, which is differently distributed and differently weighted.

adhvara.text:
The second of the two principal words for the rite, and the more particular. 241 verses against {{yajña}}'s 469. Traditional grammarians read it as *a-dhvara*, from the root *dhvṛ*, to injure — the offering that suffers no harm, that nothing breaks into. Sāyaṇa takes it that way at RV [[1.1]].4, where Agni is said to encompass the *adhvara* on every side, *viśvataḥ*: being surrounded is what keeps it whole.

Its distribution is not the same as yajña's, and the difference is worth noticing. Maṇḍala 1 and maṇḍala 8 carry 42 each; maṇḍala 3 carries 32. But **maṇḍala 2 has only three** against its sixteen occurrences of yajña. Gṛtsamada's book prefers the general word almost to the exclusion of the particular one.

Where *yajña* names the act, *adhvara* names its integrity — which is why the sūktas ask for protection of the adhvara rather than of the yajña.

ṛta.text:
The order by which things hold — the seasons turning, the waters moving, a promise kept — and in the same word, the rite that keeps them. 379 verses. To act in accordance with ṛta and to perform the offering correctly are not two different things in this vocabulary, which is why the pair {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}} can be called *ṛtāvṛdhau*, those who grow by ṛta and make it grow, in the same breath in which they are asked for rain.

The distribution has a shape. Maṇḍala 1 and maṇḍala 10 carry 71 verses each and maṇḍala 9 carries 58 — but **maṇḍala 2 carries only ten**. The concept is not evenly held across the families.

A near neighbour causes confusion and is worth separating. *Ṛta* is not *ṛtu*. **Ṛtu** is the season — the word declared in the saṅkalpa when the time of a rite is named, *ṛtau, māse, pakṣe*. They share the root √ṛ, to move or go, and the shared idea is regular recurrent motion: a season is what comes round again on time, and ṛta is the order by which anything comes round at all. The join between them is a word from the first hymn: *{{ṛtvij}}*, the officiating priest, is *ṛtu* + √yaj — one who offers at the proper season.

rayi.text:
Wealth, but wealth as sustenance rather than hoard — cattle, horses, sons, the means of keeping a household going. 277 verses, and the most frequent of the things the sūktas ask for.

Its heaviest concentration is **maṇḍala 9** (50 verses, 18%), the book given wholly to Soma Pavamāna. That is worth sitting with: the most sustained asking for wealth in the collection is addressed to the soma as it is being pressed and filtered.

It appears in the third ṛc of the first sūkta — *agninā rayim aśnavat*, through Agni one obtains rayi — where it is immediately paired with {{poṣa}}, the increase that follows, and {{yaśas}}, standing among people. The three together are what the opening asks for, and they are asked for as a set rather than singly.

The Veda is plain about wanting these things and does not apologise for wanting them. What the frame of the collection makes clear is the order of the relation: the asking sits inside the bond, not the bond inside the asking.

poṣa.text:
Nourishment, thriving, the increase that keeps a household going — from √puṣ, to make flourish. It is rare: **19 verses in the whole Ṛgveda**, fewer than any of the terms it usually travels with.

Its rarity is not a measure of its weight. It stands in the third ṛc of the first sūkta — *poṣam eva divedive*, nourishment day upon day — paired with {{rayi}} and {{yaśas}}, and that placement gives it more prominence than its frequency would suggest. The phrase it sits in, *dive-dive*, is the sūkta's own word for the rhythm of practice: not an occasional increase but a daily one.

Where {{rayi}} names the wealth, *poṣa* names its growing. A household with rayi and no poṣa has stores that are not replenishing.

yaśas.text:
Standing among people — reputation, the regard one is held in. 79 verses. Not fame in the sense of being widely known, but being well thought of by those who know you.

It belongs to the triad the first sūkta asks for. RV [[1.1]].3 puts it with {{rayi}} and {{poṣa}}: through Agni come sustenance, its increase, and *yaśas* — and then *vīravattamam*, abundance in men. The four are a picture of a household in good order, and standing is one of the four rather than a consequence of the others.

The distribution is unusually even for a term of this frequency — maṇḍala 10 carries 15, maṇḍala 1 thirteen, maṇḍala 7 twelve, and no book is without it. What a household wants of its neighbours does not vary much between families.

aṅgiras.text:
Both a name and a class. The Aṅgirases are a lineage of ṛṣis, and *aṅgiras* is also used of Agni himself — as it is in the sixth ṛc of the first sūkta, where the good Agni does for the giver is called *tavet tat satyam aṅgiraḥ*, your own truth, Aṅgiras.

Sāyaṇa explains the address by deriving the name from *aṅgāra*, a live coal, and cites the tradition preserved in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa that the coals became the Aṅgirases. That is why a fire can be spoken to by a seer's name: the two are not being confused, they are being identified.

70 verses, concentrated in maṇḍala 1 (20) and maṇḍala 10 (17) — the two books that frame the collection hold well over half of them. The Aṅgirases appear elsewhere as the ones whose singing opened the Vala cave and recovered the cattle, an episode the sūktas refer to as already known rather than narrate.

ratna.text:
Whatever is held precious — a jewel, a gift, a treasure, the good a rite returns. 107 verses. It is not the collection's word for wealth: that is {{rayi}}, which runs to 277 verses and means holdings, cattle, the means of keeping a household. *Ratna* is narrower and higher.

Its first appearance is in the first line of the Ṛgveda, in the compound *ratnadhātama* — greatest giver of ratna — which is the last of the four names RV [[1.1]].1 gives Agni. The first three are offices; this one is what he bestows. Sāyaṇa takes it figuratively there, as the reward the rite itself yields rather than as goods.

The morphology splits the compound into *ratna* and *dhātama*, and glosses the second as "giving" — so the epithet is about bestowal, not custody. Agni does not keep what is precious; he hands it on. Which is the same thing the sūkta says about the offering: what is given into him does not stay there.
